extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplar stories illustrating how to report police, crime, and court news — including initial reports, follow-ups, human-interest angles, evidence details, and investigative/sequencing information. Used to teach construction and elements of effective crime reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up stories / develop with additional information
rubrics_metrics.description: How, with additional information, a striking follow-up story can be written a few hours after the first story was published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NOTE — The book illustrates this with two stories: one appearing in the Saturday evening edition and a fuller, richer version appearing in the Sunday morning edition of the same paper. Use new facts, interviews and context obtained after the initial report to produce a more striking follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the method / modus operandi of the crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe specifically how the crime was committed (steps the perpetrator took, preparations, tricks used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: describing how a forger practiced a dairyman's name, telephoned the bank to check on checks, practiced a physician's signature, found and practiced a deposit slip signature and then cashed bad checks at named businesses. Provide sequential, concrete details so readers understand how the offense occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: State immediate facts of arrest and police action
rubrics_metrics.description: Report where and how the suspect was arrested and what the police did (detention, confession, transfer to headquarters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples list arrests at specific businesses, detention at police headquarters, detectives' names (e.g., 'taken to police headquarters and there confessed'; 'detained until the arrival of two detectives'). Include institutional and procedural details (who arrested, where, custody status).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotations to humanize and show voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Include verbatim quotes from suspects, victims, witnesses and officials to convey emotion, motive and personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "I'll pay it all back," "I never have been arrested before," statements blaming liquor, pleas for another chance, and conversational exchanges at police headquarters. Quotes can reveal motive, remorse, defiance or color and should be attributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide suspect background and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Give age, marital status, employment history, education, previous encounters with law, and personal circumstances that illuminate motive or character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include ages (16, 20, 21, 47), employment (bookkeeper, clerk, lawyer, hotel guest), family situation, prior arrests or clean records, financial strain, and anecdotes about education or social standing. These background details help readers understand pressures or surprises in the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail stolen property and its value
rubrics_metrics.description: List items taken (types and quantities) and, when available, their monetary value or sentimental importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: enumerating diamonds, emeralds, pearls, silverware, and giving total values (e.g., '$3,500' worth of jewels). Note heirloom status or sentimental value where relevant to human interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record physical evidence and clues found at scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Report forensic or physical traces (fingerprints, cigarettes, tools) that link suspects to the scene or provide leads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'A cigarette on the floor, a room full of smoke and an excellent set of finger prints on a hand mirror'—such tangible clues should be described to show investigative basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe the arrest/identification sequence and investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how suspects were identified and captured (witness descriptions, distribution of descriptions to patrols, pursuits, mistaken identity issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show witnesses giving descriptions to police, police telephoning descriptions to officers, chases, shootings leading to detentions, and complexities like uncertain identification at hospitals. Walk the reader through the chain of events from complaint to capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scene-setting and dramatic detail for engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with vivid, concrete scenes or moments that draw readers into the story (emotional reactions, small-stage drama).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a 12-year-old confronting a burglar with a revolver; a wounded bandit embraced by his wife and child in hospital; women fainting on an elevated train. Such scene details set tone and engage empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include motives, excuses or explanations offered by subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Report reasons given by suspects or others (e.g., financial pressure, liquor, family needs) and note whether authorities corroborate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where suspects say 'I was going to be married and needed money,' 'I'd been drinking for three days,' or 'I thought he persecuted me.' Present stated motives while allowing space for investigation to confirm or deny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report social/community reactions and human consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe reactions of family, friends, community leaders, clergy, and the emotional toll on relatives or victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include ministers comforting suspects' families, wives bringing clothing to jail, neighbors' shock, or hysterical victims taken to hospital. These details contextualize the event's social impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide institutional and legal context (charges, hearings)
rubrics_metrics.description: State intended or pending charges, arraignment plans, jail status, and relevant legal steps following arrest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'will be charged with a felony,' held overnight, to be arraigned when physically able. Include prosecutorial statements and immediate legal outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft human-interest angles within crime reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, frame the incident around a relatable human story (hard luck, desperation, heroism) to broaden reader interest beyond the crime itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: stories emphasizing 'hard-luck' causes for crime (illness, unemployment), a child's bravery in confronting a burglar, or the domestic fallout for families. Use such angles ethically to inform and engage.
